transcript.content: Hello, I’m Dr. ____. What brings you in today?

Well, doctor, I guess I’m here because... well, it really all started back when I got that county safety award. You’d think getting recognized for doing your job well—I'm a transportation inspector, by the way, making sure everything is up to code and safe for the public—you'd think an award would be a good thing, right? A point of pride. But honestly, ever since they handed me that certificate, things have just gotten completely out of hand at the office. 

Certain people... and I know exactly who they are, but certain people at work have been taking my inspection reports and completely twisting them around. I write everything down exactly to protocol, I'm very thorough, but they’ll take a standard notation and try to make it sound like I missed a defect, or they’ll start asking me these incredibly pointed budget questions. Questions that they have no business asking me, but they ask them in this very specific, calculating way, like they’re trying to trap me. Like they’re trying to make me look crooked or on the take or something. 

And I’ve tried explaining this to my supervisor. I sat down with him and laid it all out, showed him the discrepancies in how they were treating my files, but he just waves it off. He keeps telling me that it is just a normal review and that I shouldn't worry about it. But I know what a normal review looks like, I've been doing this long enough, and this isn't it. I can tell, plain as day, that there is a coordinated effort going on behind my back to discredit me and ruin my reputation, and it's just exhausting trying to stay one step ahead of them.
How long have you been feeling that people at work are trying to discredit you?

Well, if I really sit down and trace it back—and believe me, I have, I've spent a lot of nights just going over the timeline in my head trying to pinpoint the exact moment the atmosphere in the office shifted—it’s been going on for about a year now. A full year of this constant... maneuvering. 

It all ties directly back to that county safety initiative I was telling you about. Before that, you know, I was just doing my job, running my routes, checking the structural integrity of the overpasses, making sure the contractors weren't cutting corners on the materials and the guardrails. Just doing the hard work that keeps people safe. But then I got recognized for that initiative about twelve months ago, and almost immediately, I mean literally within a couple of weeks of them handing me that piece of paper, the whole vibe changed. 

I remember the very first time it happened, actually. It was right after a Tuesday morning stand-up meeting—we always do our weekly briefs on Tuesdays—and someone made this incredibly sly, underhanded comment about one of my field reports. Just testing the waters, you know? Seeing if I'd notice. So, yeah, it’s been about a year. Twelve solid months of them digging through my logs, second-guessing my budget numbers, and just waiting for me to make one tiny little clerical mistake so they can tear down everything I've built. It doesn't stop, doctor, it's just been a year of looking over my shoulder every time I file a piece of paperwork.
Have you heard or seen things that other people don’t seem to hear or see?

No, no, nothing like that. I mean, I know what you're getting at—you're asking if I'm hallucinating, right? If I'm seeing ghosts or hearing voices whispering in my ear. But no, I don't have any of that going on. My hearing is perfectly fine, my eyesight is 20/20—well, maybe 20/25 in the left eye, but I just had my DOT physical a few months ago and passed with flying colors. So I'm not imagining things. 

What I'm talking about is real, tangible stuff. It's the way they look at me when I walk into the breakroom, or the sudden silence when I turn a corner. Or the actual, physical paperwork. Like, if you were to look at the routing slips on my inspection files, you'd see the extra initials, the secondary review stamps that nobody else gets. That's not me hearing things, that's just me paying attention to the details. Which is my job, right? I'm trained to spot anomalies. If a bridge support has a hairline fracture, I have to see it. If a contractor is trying to pass off grade-B steel as grade-A, I have to catch it. So when they start pulling this kind of subtle sabotage in the office, of course I'm going to notice it. I don't need to be hearing voices to know when someone is trying to pull the rug out from under me. I just need to read the room and read the reports. So, no, I'm not seeing things that aren't there. I'm just seeing the things they're trying to hide.
Do you think there is any chance that your coworkers' actions might be a misunderstanding or a normal work review, rather than a deliberate plot against you?

I mean, I get why you'd ask that. It’s the logical question, right? And honestly, I’ve asked myself the exact same thing. I’ve laid awake at night, staring at the ceiling, just running through every interaction, every email, every little comment, trying to see if maybe, just maybe, I’m overreacting. But then I go back into the office the next day, and the pattern is just too clear. It’s not just a misunderstanding. You don’t get a misunderstanding this consistent, this targeted, day in and day out. 

Like I said, it all traces back to that county safety award. Before that, everything was fine. Normal reviews were just normal reviews. But ever since I got that recognition, they’ve been taking my inspection reports—reports that I write exactly to protocol, down to the letter—and twisting them. They’ll pull out a standard notation and try to make it look like I missed a critical defect, or they’ll start grilling me with these incredibly pointed budget questions. And it’s the way they ask them, you know? It’s not a casual, "Hey, can you clarify this expense?" It’s calculating. It’s designed to trap me, to make me look like I’m crooked or skimming off the top. 

And my supervisor, he does exactly what you’re doing right now—he tries to tell me it’s just a normal review. I sat down with him, I brought the files, I showed him the discrepancies, the extra scrutiny that nobody else gets. And he just waves it off. He says, "Don't worry about it, it's just standard procedure." But I know standard procedure. I’ve been a transportation inspector for years. I know what a normal review looks like, and I know what a witch hunt looks like. When you’re trained to spot anomalies, to find the hairline fractures in a bridge support or the cut corners in a contractor's materials, you learn to trust your eyes. And my eyes are telling me that this isn't a misunderstanding. There is a coordinated, deliberate effort going on behind my back to discredit me and ruin my reputation. I can see it plain as day, even if nobody else wants to admit it.
Aside from this situation at work, do you think anything else unusual or suspicious is happening to you?

No, honestly, no. And I think... well, I think that’s a really important point to make here, actually. Outside of the office, my life is completely, one hundred percent normal. I mean, I go home, I tinker with my truck, I watch the game on Sundays. I go to the grocery store and nobody is looking at me sideways. The cashier just scans my milk and bread and says have a good day. There’s no... there's no grand conspiracy at the gas station when I fill up, you know? My neighbor, he's just a regular guy, we talk about lawn care and the weather over the fence. I don't think he's spying on me or anything crazy like that. 

And see, doctor, that’s exactly how I know I’m right about what’s happening at work. If I were just making things up, or if I were just some generally paranoid person, wouldn't I think the mailman was following me? Wouldn't I think everyone on the street was out to get me? But I don't. Because they aren't. It’s strictly confined to the department. It’s only my coworkers and my supervisor, because they’re the only ones who actually have a stake in this. They’re the ones who felt shown up by that safety award. The rest of the world couldn't care less about county bridge inspection protocols or guardrail material specs. 

So, no, absolutely nothing unusual is happening anywhere else in my life. I sleep fine, I pay my bills, I go about my business. It’s just that one specific, very real, very documented situation at my job. That's the only place where the math isn't adding up.
Have you had any period when your thoughts felt racing or your speech felt unusually fast?

No, no, nothing like that. I mean, my thoughts are just... they're just normal thoughts, you know? They don't race. I'm a very methodical person. You have to be, in my line of work. When you're inspecting a suspension cable or checking the torque on a load-bearing bolt, you can't have a million things flying through your head at a hundred miles an hour. You have to be focused. You have to take it step by step, item by item on the checklist. And that's exactly how my mind works. It's organized. It's deliberate. 

And as for my speech, well, I know I'm talking a lot right now, but that's just because I need to make sure you have all the facts. I need to make sure you understand the full context of what I'm dealing with at the office, because if I just give you a yes or no answer, you might get the wrong idea. But my speech isn't unusually fast or anything. I'm not tripping over my words or rambling out of control. I'm just explaining things thoroughly. 

I've never had a time where I felt like my brain was on overdrive or anything like that. Even when I'm stressed out about the sabotage at work, even when I'm sitting there looking at a routing slip that's been clearly tampered with, my thoughts don't race. They just focus in on the problem. I analyze it, I document it, and I figure out my next move. It's very logical. It's very calm, actually, considering what they're putting me through. So, no, no racing thoughts, no fast talking. Just a guy trying to do his job and protect his livelihood from people who are trying to tear it down.
How certain are you that your coworkers are deliberately targeting you—could you be convinced otherwise if shown clear evidence?

How certain am I? I mean... I am one hundred percent certain. I don't think there's even a fraction of a doubt in my mind at this point. You ask if clear evidence could convince me otherwise, but... well, you have to understand, the evidence is exactly what I've been talking about. Like I said before, the whole reason I'm even dealing with this, the reason I'm here, is because ever since I got that county safety award, I have been watching the evidence pile up right in front of my own eyes. 

If someone brought me a piece of paper right now claiming to be evidence that this is all just a big misunderstanding, I'd have to ask who manufactured it, you know? Because I'm the one looking at my own inspection reports every single day. I write them up, perfectly to code, doing my job exactly the way I was trained, and then I watch certain people at work take those exact documents and twist them around. They take a standard observation about a guardrail or a drainage culvert and blow it completely out of proportion, and then they come at me with those pointed budget questions I mentioned earlier. They'll pull up a requisition form from three months ago and interrogate me over a fifty-dollar equipment variance, just... just pushing and pushing, trying to make me look crooked. Trying to make it seem like I'm incompetent or skimming off the department. 

So what evidence could possibly undo that? I mean, what could you show me that changes the reality of what they are doing to my paperwork? I've already tried to look for an alternative explanation myself. I took it all to my supervisor, hoping he'd look at the files and say, oh, I see what's happening here, let's fix this. But even when I lay it all out for him, he just brushes it off and says it’s just a normal review process. But I know it's not. I've been an inspector since I was right out of high school. I can tell there’s a coordinated effort to discredit me, and it's happening right out in the open if you just know how to read the routing slips and the email chains. So, no, I couldn't be convinced otherwise, because the real, actual proof of what they're doing is already sitting right there in my filing cabinet at work.
Has this belief ever led you to avoid going to work, miss shifts, or have trouble functioning on the job?

No, no, I haven't missed a single day. Not one. I mean, if I start calling out sick or showing up late, that's just giving them exactly what they want, isn't it? They'd love to write me up for absenteeism. So, no, I am there every morning, ten minutes early, coffee in hand, ready to go. I still get to work on time, I still do my inspections exactly by the book—probably better than anyone else in the county, to be honest, because I know they're scrutinizing every single measurement I take. 

And it hasn't stopped me from doing the rest of my life, either. Like I was saying before, everything else is totally normal. I still go to church on Sundays, sit in the same pew I always do. I still take care of myself, keep my house clean, pay my bills. The functioning part... I mean, I'm functioning perfectly fine. I'm doing the job. I'm doing the work. 

The only time things get... difficult... is when they force the issue. The main problems only really come up when we have those department meetings, or when someone brings up one of those altered reports, or when they start questioning my spending on the requisition forms. That's when it gets tense. Because I have to defend myself, right? I have to stand there and explain why a fifty-dollar variance on safety harnesses is completely standard, while they all sit around the table looking at me like I'm trying to rob the county blind. 

So, yeah, it's stressful. It's incredibly stressful to have to constantly watch your back and document every single conversation just to prove you aren't crazy or incompetent. But it hasn't stopped me from doing my job. I won't let it. I refuse to let them push me out of a career I've been building since I was eighteen years old just because they're jealous of a safety award. I just keep my head down, do the inspections, and make sure my paperwork is absolutely bulletproof.
Have you generally been suspicious of other people and slow to trust them for most of your adult life?

No, no, not at all. Actually, it's funny you ask that, because people who know me—like the guys I went to high school with, or my neighbors—they'd tell you I'm a pretty open book. I've never been the kind of guy who looks over his shoulder or thinks everyone is out to get him. I mean, I've got buddies I've known for ten years where we share tools, help each other out with truck repairs, and I don't think twice about it. I trust them completely. 

And honestly, even at work, before all this started, before I got that county safety award, I trusted my coworkers, too! I really did. I'd leave my lunch in the breakroom fridge, I'd leave my clipboard on the dashboard of the county truck with the windows rolled down while I was checking a site, and I never worried about it. I was always the first guy to spot someone a few bucks for the vending machine if they were short, or cover a shift if someone's kid was sick. I just figured we were all on the same team, you know? Keeping the roads and bridges safe. In this line of work, you kind of have to trust the guy holding the other end of the tape measure or spotting you on a steep grade. 

So, no, I'm not some... some suspicious hermit who thinks the whole world is bad. I've never been like that. And I think that's why this whole thing with the inspection reports and the requisition forms is so incredibly frustrating for me. Because I *want* to trust people. I *did* trust them. But when you're sitting there watching people you thought were on your side actively taking your perfectly good paperwork and twisting it to make you look like a fool, well... obviously, I can't trust *them* anymore. I'd be an idiot to trust them after what they've done. 

But out in the real world? Outside of that department? No, I trust people just fine. I'm a very straightforward guy. If you're straight with me, I'm straight with you. It's really just this specific group of people at the office who have decided to make my life miserable because they couldn't handle me getting a little bit of recognition. So, no, I've never had a problem trusting people in general, not at all.
Have you had this kind of suspicion and distrust toward other people for as long as you can remember, even before this situation at work started?

No, no, definitely not for as long as I can remember. Like I was just saying, I've always been a pretty trusting guy. I mean, growing up, through high school, my early twenties... I never had any issues with people. I never thought anyone was out to get me or anything like that. I was just a regular guy, doing my thing, you know? 

This whole situation, this... this nightmare at work... it really only started about a year ago. Yeah, I'd say it's been right around twelve months now. It all tracks back to that exact same thing I keep telling you about—the county safety initiative. I had been working hard, putting in the hours, making sure every single site I inspected was up to par, and the county recognized that. They gave me the award. And you'd think that would be a good thing, right? You'd think people would be happy for you, maybe give you a pat on the back, say 'good job.' 

But no, that's exactly when it all shifted. That's when the atmosphere in the office just... changed. I remember it so clearly. It was maybe a week or two after the award ceremony, and I started noticing the little things. The way people would stop talking when I walked into the breakroom, the weird looks, the sudden interest in my requisition forms. And then, of course, the altered reports. That's when I realized what was happening. So, yeah, it's been about a year of this constant, grinding pressure, just having to defend myself every single day. But before that? No, never. I trusted them. I trusted everyone. It's just this past year that they've proven I can't.
Before this year at work, would you say you’ve generally been wary of other people and quick to suspect bad motives in day-to-day life?

Look, I feel like we're just going in circles here, Doc. Like I just said, no. Absolutely not. I wasn't walking around looking for the bad in people. 

You know, before all this started, if a guy cut me off in traffic on the way to a site, I'd just think, hey, maybe he's late for work, not that he's trying to run me off the road. If the cashier at the hardware store shorted me a dime on my change when I was buying zip ties or whatever, I just figured it was a simple math mistake, not some... some scheme to rip me off. I was just a regular guy taking things at face value. I'd go down to the diner, sit at the counter, talk to whoever was there about the football game or the weather, and I never once thought anyone had some ulterior motive. If a guy asked how my day was, I just thought he was being polite. People were just people. 

I didn't have the energy or the mindset to be constantly analyzing everyone's motives. Life was simple, you know? I'd wake up, do my inspections, go home, watch some TV, maybe barbecue on the weekend with the neighbors. I didn't spend my evenings wondering who was talking behind my back because, frankly, I didn't think anyone cared enough to do it! There was zero reason to be wary of anyone because no one was actively messing with my life back then. I didn't have to check and re-check my own files just to make sure someone hadn't slipped in a bogus invoice. 

So, to answer your question again... no. I was never quick to suspect bad motives in my day-to-day life. I was probably too trusting, if anything. I just expected people to do their jobs and be decent, and it wasn't until this whole safety award thing that they literally handed me a reason to think otherwise.
Have you ever had similar suspicions about people in other settings, outside of work?

No, I haven't. And honestly, it's getting a little frustrating that you keep asking me the same basic question in five different ways. I mean, I'm trying to be patient here, I really am, because I know you have your checklist or whatever it is you need to get through, but I feel like I've been pretty clear. 

Outside of work? No. Never. Not at the grocery store, not at the mechanic, not with my family, not with the guys I play softball with on Thursdays. I've never had any reason to think anyone was out to get me or sabotage me in those places because, well, they aren't! My brother-in-law isn't sneaking into my house to mess with my electric bill, you know? The guy at the deli isn't shorting me on pastrami because he's jealous of me. Life outside of the county transportation department is completely normal. 

It's just that one specific office. That one specific group of people who couldn't handle the fact that I got recognized for doing my job well. That's the only place this is happening. So, no, I don't have these... these suspicions everywhere I go. I'm not crazy. I'm just a guy who's dealing with a very real, very targeted harassment campaign at his workplace, and I just wish someone would actually listen to me about that instead of trying to make it sound like I've got some lifelong problem with trusting people. Because I don't. I really, really don't.
Do you feel suspicious or mistrustful of your boss in particular, or of most people in authority?

Well, see, that's the thing. It's not about "people in authority" as some big, general concept. I don't have a problem with authority. If a cop pulls me over for speeding, I hand him my license and registration, say 'yes sir,' 'no sir,' and pay the ticket. I respect the chain of command. I really do. 

But my boss... Mr. Henderson... that's a whole different story. It's not that I'm suspicious of him *because* he's the boss. I'm suspicious of him because of how he's handling this whole mess. Or, rather, how he's *not* handling it. I mean, I've gone to him. I've brought him the altered requisition forms. I've shown him the discrepancies in the site logs where someone clearly went in after me and changed my notes. I laid it all out on his desk, right there in front of him, plain as day. And what does he do? He just sighs, rubs his temples, and tells me I'm "overthinking things" or that it's just "administrative errors." 

Administrative errors? Come on. You don't accidentally swap a passing grade for a failing one on a structural support beam inspection. That doesn't just happen because someone hit the wrong key on a keyboard. But Henderson... he just brushes it off. And that's what makes me wonder. Because he's not a stupid guy. He's been the regional director for fifteen years. He knows how the system works. So if he's ignoring evidence that's right in front of his face, you have to ask yourself why. 

Is he in on it? Did the guys in the office get to him? Or maybe he's just turning a blind eye because he doesn't want the paperwork of dealing with a whole department that's actively trying to sabotage one of their own inspectors. I don't know for sure. But I do know that when the guy in charge refuses to stop the people under him from messing with my career, I can't trust him. I just can't. It's not about authority, Doc. It's about him specifically, and the fact that he's either complicit or completely incompetent when it comes to what's happening to me.
If someone showed you clear, convincing proof that your coworkers were not targeting you, would you be able to accept that?

Clear, convincing proof? Doc, I... I don't even know how to answer that because it's like asking me if I'd accept proof that the sky is green. I mean, what kind of proof could someone possibly show me that would erase everything that's actually happening? 

Think about it from my perspective. I’m only even sitting here in this chair talking to you because ever since I got that county safety award—which, by the way, I didn't even ask for, they just handed it to me at the annual banquet because my site compliance was at a hundred percent for three years straight—ever since that exact moment, the target has been on my back. Certain people at work, guys I used to share a thermos of coffee with at the depot, they started twisting my inspection reports. I'd write down that a retaining wall needed a class-three reinforcement, and suddenly the digitized file says I marked it as perfectly fine. 

And then comes the money stuff. They started pulling me into these little impromptu meetings, asking these really pointed budget questions. "Why did you allocate this much for concrete testing on the highway 9 project?" or "Are you sure you didn't over-order on the road flares?" They ask it in this tone, you know, like they’re trying to make me look crooked. Like I'm skimming off the top or taking kickbacks from the contractors! I've been a transportation inspector for seven years, I make a decent living, I drive a 2014 Ford F-150, I don't need to steal from the county! 

And when I try to point this out, when I take these altered reports and these ridiculous budget inquiries to my supervisor, he just gives me this tired look and says it’s just "normal review." He tells me everyone gets audited, it's just standard procedure for award-winners. Standard procedure? To secretly change my structural notes? Give me a break. 

So, no. If someone came to me with a piece of paper or some HR document claiming to be "proof" that they aren't targeting me, I wouldn't accept it, because it would just be another lie. I know what I'm experiencing. I can tell there’s a coordinated effort to discredit me, to ruin my reputation and probably get me fired so they can give my route to someone else. You can't prove to me that a fire isn't hot when I'm the one standing in the flames, you know what I mean?
If you were presented with strong proof that your coworkers were not targeting you, would you be able to accept it?

I mean, doc, we... we literally just went over this. It's like you're not even hearing me. You're asking the exact same thing again, just using the word "strong" instead of "clear and convincing." Strong proof? What does that even look like? A notarized letter from the guys who are actively trying to ruin my life saying, "Hey, we promise we aren't doing the thing we're totally doing"? 

Look, I'm here... I'm sitting in this office talking to you right now... because ever since I got that county safety award, the one they just handed to me at the banquet, certain people at work have been twisting my inspection reports. That's a fact. That's not something you can just wave away with some imaginary "proof." I write down a class-three reinforcement requirement, and the file gets changed. And then they start pulling me into these meetings, asking these really pointed budget questions, you know? Like they’re trying to make me look crooked, like I'm skimming off the top of the highway 9 project or something. 

And even when I bring all of this... the changed reports, the weird questions... when I bring it all to my supervisor, he just gives me this look and says it’s just "normal review." He says everybody gets audited. But I can tell there’s a coordinated effort to discredit me. It's obvious. They want to ruin my reputation. So, no, I wouldn't accept this "strong proof" because it wouldn't be real. I'm living it, doc. I don't need proof that it's not happening when I can clearly see that it is.
